sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Patients with recurrent endometrial or ovarian cancer have poor survival outcomes. We evaluated the clinical efficacy and toxicity of copanlisib [a phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor] and niraparib [a poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi)] in this patient population with translational insights.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: This was a phase Ib trial. Copanlisib was administered intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day cycle, and niraparib was given orally once daily. Four dose levels were explored over a dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) window of 28 days. The primary objective was to determine the recommended phase II dose (RP2D) of this combination. Secondary objectives included safety, objective response rate (ORR), and pharmacokinetics. Tumor biopsies were analyzed using reverse phase protein array (RPPA) to identify molecular correlates of response.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Thirty patients were enrolled. An RP2D was not established due to DLTs, most commonly a grade 3 maculopapular rash attributed to copanlisib. The ORR was 12.5% (95% confidence interval, 2.8%–33.6%). RPPA was performed on tumors from eight patients. PI3K pathway activity did not correlate with PI3K mutational status. Nineteen proteins were differentially expressed between patients with stable disease and those with progressive disease; many were substrates of Akt (protein kinase B), implicating downstream PI3K signaling in response.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: The combination of copanlisib and niraparib demonstrated limited tolerability, and the ORR was modest. However, functional proteomic analyses identified candidate biomarkers—particularly Akt pathway substrates—which may inform future strategies to optimize PI3K and PARPi combinations.

boxed-text.p: This clinical trial evaluated the efficacy and toxicity of copanlisib, a phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor, and niraparib, a poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi), in patients with recurrent ovarian or endometrial cancer. In parallel, the molecular profile of tumors was explored to determine if early changes in functional proteomic biomarkers in tumor biopsies before and during treatment were associated with response to therapy. This demonstrated that PI3K pathway activation within tumors was not directly correlated with PI3K mutation status. However, a combination of phosphorylation of Akt substrates and ARID1A levels may serve as a promising biomarker for a combination of PI3K inhibitors and PARPis in the future.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Ovarian cancer (encompassing ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancers) has been the deadliest gynecologic malignancy in the United States for decades (1). Although patients with ovarian cancer often achieve remission with initial treatment of cytoreductive surgery followed by platinum- and taxane-based chemotherapy, most patients will relapse and eventually die of their disease (2). The proportion of deaths relative to new diagnoses is still the highest of all gynecologic malignancies. Treatment for recurrent ovarian cancer is determined by platinum sensitivity and the time from the last platinum-based chemotherapy to recurrence. For patients with platinum-sensitive disease, defined as >6 months from the last platinum dose to recurrence, preferred regimens include platinum-based therapy combined with either gemcitabine, liposomal doxorubicin, or paclitaxel, with or without the addition of bevacizumab (3–8). For patients with platinum-resistant disease, preferred treatment regimens include mirvetuximab for folate receptor alpha–positive tumors, trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2 3+ expressing tumors, docetaxel, gemcitabine, liposomal doxorubicin, paclitaxel, and topotecan, with or without the addition of bevacizumab (9–16). Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) have also been shown to be effective as a maintenance strategy for BRCA-mutated or homologous recombination deficient (HRD) platinum-sensitive ovarian cancers although the preference is to give these agents as early as possible in the treatment continuum (17–19). Although there are numerous options for the treatment of relapsed ovarian cancer, ovarian cancer remains overall incurable.

Endometrial cancer is often diagnosed at earlier stages with a high rate of cure; however, in 2024, it surpassed ovarian cancer as the deadliest gynecologic malignancy in the United States (1, 20). However, patients with recurrent disease have poor survival outcomes. Preferred regimens for recurrent disease include a combination of carboplatin and paclitaxel with either immunotherapy or trastuzumab (for HER2-expressing tumors) or lenvatinib and pembrolizumab (21–25). There is limited benefit from chemotherapy in patients with endometrial cancer who have progressed after first-line treatment (26, 27). Novel therapeutics are urgently needed to improve outcomes for patients with recurrent ovarian or endometrial cancer.

The phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway is a prominent signal transduction cascade that promotes cellular survival and is constitutively activated in many types of cancers (28, 29). The tumor suppressor phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) antagonizes PI3K by dephosphorylating PIP3, and its activity is frequently lost in cancer cells (30). In addition to promoting the survival of tumor cells, activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway facilitates resistance to the effects of cytotoxic chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted agents such as trastuzumab (26, 31). Given these critical roles in tumor progression, PI3K inhibitors have been hypothesized to be effective against PI3K pathway–driven tumors and in combination with other chemotherapy agents. Targeting the PI3K pathway, and subsequently the consequences of PTEN loss, is a potential therapeutic option for both endometrial and ovarian cancer. More than 80% of endometrial cancers have aberrations in PTEN, making this an actionable target (32). Furthermore, the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway is active in both endometrial and high-grade serous ovarian cancers, with PI3K or AKT mutations or amplification present in a subset of tumors (33–35). For these reasons, therapies that target the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway in these cancers are of increasing interest.

BRCA mutations are common in ovarian cancers, with 13% to 15% of cases having germline mutations and 7% with somatic mutations (36). HRD is also present in 30% of ovarian cancers that are negative for either germline or somatic BRCA mutations (36). PARP-1 and PARP-2 are enzymes involved in the base excision repair of single-strand DNA breaks (SSB). Inhibition of PARP leads to unrepaired SSBs, which result in double-strand breaks during DNA replication. Further PARP inhibition induces replication fork collapse and traps PARP on DNA, resulting in DNA damage. The combination of PARP inhibition with defective homologous recombination leads to enhanced cell death, a concept termed “synthetic lethality” (37). PARP inhibition induces synthetic lethality in tumor cells bearing BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, both of which are key components in the pathway of repair for DNA double-strand breaks, and in tumors with defective homologous recombination (38, 39). PTEN is also involved in maintaining genomic stability, and PTEN mutations lead to defects in homologous recombination, which is crucial for repairing double-strand DNA breaks (40). Therefore, both PARPi and therapies that target the PI3K pathway and thus affect PTEN are of interest.

Niraparib is a potent and specific inhibitor of PARP-1 and PARP-2, with activity in tumor cell lines bearing DNA repair deficiencies (18, 41). Niraparib is currently FDA-approved for maintenance therapy in ovarian cancer. Copanlisib is a potent pan–class I inhibitor targeting PI3Kα, PI3Kδ, and PI3Kγ (42, 43). Copanlisib is currently FDA-approved for the treatment of relapsed follicular lymphoma. Preclinical cell line and animal model data demonstrate that PI3K pathway inhibitors are synergistic with PARPi in both in vitro and in vivo models (44, 45). This activity, combined with the concept of potential synthetic lethality, makes this combination attractive for ovarian and endometrial cancer. This study presents the results of a phase Ib clinical trial of niraparib and copanlisib in patients with recurrent endometrial and ovarian cancers. This trial sought to determine the recommended phase II dose (RP2D) and to assess the safety and clinical activity of this drug combination.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: COPANIRA (NCT03586661) is a phase Ib, single-center, open-label study evaluating the combination of niraparib and copanlisib in patients with recurrent endometrial or ovarian cancer. The primary objective was to determine the maximum tolerated dose and the RP2D of niraparib in combination with copanlisib in patients with recurrent high-grade serous ovarian cancer, BRCA-mutant ovarian cancer with no curative option available, or recurrent endometrial cancer. Secondary objectives included determining the tolerability and toxicity of the drug combination, the drug combination activity by objective response rate (ORR), the response duration, and the pharmacokinetics (PK) of the combination (Fig. 1). Additionally, translational analyses were conducted to explore the association between therapeutic response and tumor molecular profiles.

caption.p: Study schema. ECOG, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group.

sec.p: The study was conducted using a dose escalation model with a Bayesian Optimal Interval design (46, 47); dose re-escalations were not permitted (Supplementary Table S1). Three patients were initially enrolled at dose level 1 (DL1), and subsequent patients were treated in cohorts of three. If no dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) occurred in a group of three, dose escalation occurred. If one DLT occurred in a group of three, an additional three were added. If two DLTs occurred in a group of three, dose de-escalation occurred.

Subsequently, a dose expansion cohort at the RP2D was conducted to further evaluate PK (exposure–response analyses) and translational data. The expansion cohort planned to enroll 20 patients: 10 with ovarian cancer and 10 with endometrial cancer. The same inclusion criteria were applied as in the dose escalation group, with the addition of two criteria (Fig. 1). All patients enrolled in the expansion cohort had to be willing to undergo pre- and on-treatment biopsies. Patients received oral niraparib on days 1 to 28 once daily and intravenous copanlisib on days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day cycle. Four DLs were planned (Fig. 1). Dose modifications and interruptions were allowed for both drugs.

sec.title: Patient selection
sec.p: Eligible patients had a histologically confirmed diagnosis of recurrent endometrial adenocarcinoma (excluding carcinosarcoma) or recurrent high-grade serous ovarian cancer (Fig. 1). Patients could have received unlimited prior therapeutic regimens for their cancer. For the dose escalation cohort, patients with ovarian cancer were required to have platinum-resistant disease, defined as progression within 6 months from the completion of platinum-based therapy and prior progression on a PARPi if BRCA-mutated or HRD. Prior PARP or PI3K pathway inhibitors were allowed. However, prior use of PI3K pathway inhibitors made patients only eligible for the dose escalation phase.

sec.title: Compliance and ethical standards
sec.p: This study, NCI Protocol 2017-0404, involving human participants, was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki of 1964 and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards and was approved by the center’s Institutional Review Board. Written informed consent was obtained from all individual participants.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: Safety assessments were conducted weekly during the first month and then monthly thereafter. Toxicities were assessed using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 5.0; ref. 48). DLTs were defined as a treatment-related toxic effect occurring during the first 4 weeks of therapy and consisted of any grade 4 hematologic or grade 3 to 4 nonhematologic toxicity (except grade 3 nausea/vomiting or diarrhea that improved within 3 days of treatment, grade 3 hyperglycemia with improvement with the initiation of insulin, elevated blood pressure >150/90 mmHg with improvement within 3 days with or without medication), any delay of treatment >2 weeks, any incidence of Hy’s law, and any grade of infectious pneumonitis or pancreatitis. If patients could not take at least 75% of the planned dose in cycle 1 due to drug-related toxicity, this was also considered a DLT.

Dose modifications and interruptions were implemented based on specific guidelines in the protocol. Broadly, adverse events (AE) that were grade 3 or higher required dose interruption until resolution of toxicity to grade 1. Dose reductions were required if the AE did not resolve within 7 days. A delay in therapy was permitted for up to 21 days. Patients with nonhematologic grade 4 toxicities were discontinued from the study. Dose re-escalation was not permitted after resolution of toxicity.

Patients were assessed for tumor response via imaging every two cycles (8 weeks) for the first 6 months, and then assessment was extended to every three cycles. Disease response and progression were evaluated using the RECIST version 1.1 guidelines and criteria (49). In the expansion cohort, patients underwent blood draws and biopsies for correlative testing prior to the start of therapy, after one cycle of treatment, and at the time of progression.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic, clinical, and AEs for the treated subjects. We estimated the ORR and clinical benefit rate (CBR) along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). CBR is defined as an objective response or stable disease (SD) for four or more cycles. For patients with clinical benefit, the duration of response (DOR) was calculated from the start of treatment to progression on imaging. All statistical analyses were performed using Stata/MP version 17.0.

sec.title: Translational analysis
sec.p: Tumor biopsies were collected from patients prior to treatment initiation and after 28 days on therapy for patients in the expansion cohort. Reverse phase protein array (RPPA) analysis was performed using frozen tumor specimens (RRID:SCR_016649; ref. 50). We assessed the phosphorylation status of proteins using antibodies specific to certain proteins or their phosphorylated forms. Phosphoprotein measurements were not normalized to their corresponding total protein levels as the analysis was designed to assess absolute phosphoprotein abundance; all values reflect globally normalized signals processed by the MD Anderson Cancer Center RPPA core facility. This approach was employed because most antibodies used in RPPA analyses are preselected for signaling pathways that are well established as being involved in tumor development. For the construction of a PI3K score, we used average RPPA signals from antibodies against eleven proteins in the PI3K pathway (Akt_PT308, Akt1_pS473, Akt_pS473, GSK-3-a/b_pS21_S9, Rictor_pT1135, mTOR_pS2448, p70-S6K_pT389, p90RSK_pT573, S6_pS240/S244, S6_pS235/236, and 4EBP1_pT34/46). Differential protein expression between the SD and progressive disease (PD) groups was carried out using the Student t test. For pathway analysis, we identified pathways enriched in all genes corresponding to RPPA proteins using the R (RRID:SCR_001905) clusterProfiler package (RRID:SCR_016884) and MSigDB (RRID: SCR_016863). Only C2 curated and hallmark gene sets were used (https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb). Twenty-eight top pathways were compiled based on gene sets from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, Reactome, Gene Ontology, and Hallmark pathways. The AKT substrates pathway was added based on a listing from Cell Signaling Technology (https://www.cellsignal.com/learn-and-support/reference-tables/pi3k-akt-substrates-table). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was then performed using the R fgsea package (RRID: SCR_020938) on 29 constructed RPPA pathways (Supplementary Table S2).

Whole-exome DNA sequencing (WES) was performed at the MD Anderson Cancer Genomics Core Laboratory (RRID: SCR_026237) according to the following procedures. Genomic DNA (gDNA) was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (QIAGEN, RRID:SCR_008539), quantified with the Quant-iT PicoGreen dsDNA Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, RRID:SCR_008452), and assessed for quality using the Genomic DNA ScreenTape and Reagents on the TapeStation 4200 (Agilent Technologies, RRID:SCR_013575). Up to 200 ng of each gDNA sample, based on PicoGreen quantification, was sheared with the E220 Focused-ultrasonicator (Covaris, RRID:SCR_019817) under the following conditions: peak incident power 200, duty cycle 25%, cycles per burst 50, for 10 seconds, repeated for 70 iterations. Fragment size was verified on the TapeStation 4200 using the DNA High Sensitivity kit (Agilent Technologies, RRID:SCR_013575). Library preparation was performed using the Agilent (RRID:SCR_013575) SureSelect XT HS2 DNA Reagent Kit with 384 unique dual sample indexing and dual molecular barcodes to reduce false positives and improve detection of low variant allele frequencies (VAF). The protocol included end repair, A-tailing, and adaptor ligation, followed by barcode insertion via PCR with Herculase II Fusion DNA Polymerase (8–14 cycles, depending on DNA quality and quantity, RRID:SCR_013575). PCR primers were removed using 1× volume of the Agencourt AMPure PCR Purification kit (Agencourt Bioscience Corporation, RRID:SCR_008940). Library quality and quantity were evaluated on the TapeStation 4200 with the DNA High Sensitivity kit (RRID:SCR_013575).

Libraries were individually hybridized to Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon version 4 probes (Agilent Technologies, RRID:SCR_013575) using the Sciclone G3 NGSx Workstation (PerkinElmer Inc., RRID: SCR_018621), with 500 to 1,000 ng of prepared library per sample. Hybridization and posthybridization capture and washes were performed according to Agilent’s protocol. Sequencing was conducted on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform (RRID: SCR_016387) with 2 × 150 paired-end reads and an 8 nt index read, using Cycle Sequencing version 1.5 reagents (Illumina). Demultiplexing was performed with Illumina’s bcl2fastq or BCL Convert software (RRID:SCR_015058, RRID:SCR_021202), generating paired-end reads based on dual indexes and removing incorrectly paired P5 and P7 indexes. Molecular barcode extraction and trimming were done using the Agilent Genomics NextGen Toolkit (RRID:SCR_013575). Trimmed BCL files were converted to “.fastq.gz” format and demultiplexed using CASAVA 1.8.2 (RRID: SCR_001802) with no mismatches. Coverage was ensured to be >20 reads per region. For data analysis, we aligned the whole exome sequencing capture deep sequencing data to the hg19 human reference assembly using BWA (RRID:SCR_010910; ref. 51) and removed duplicate reads with Picard (RRID:SCR_006525; ref. 52). Single-nucleotide variants and small indels were identified using an in-house pipeline (53), classifying variants into somatic, germline, and loss of heterozygosity categories based on VAF in tumor and matched normal tissues. VCF files were converted to MAF files and analyzed by the R oncoplot (RRID: SCR_024519) package.

sec.title: PK sampling and assay (exposure–response analysis)
sec.p: PK analysis was conducted on day 15 of cycle 1 for both copanlisib (parent and M1 metabolite) and niraparib. From consented patients, limited blood sampling for the determination of drug concentrations was collected before the dose and at 55 minutes, 1.5, 5, and 24 hours from the start of dose administration. Additional samples were collected before the dose and at 55 minutes from the start of dose administration on day 15 of cycles 3 and 6. Following good clinical and laboratory practices, blood was collected into K2-EDTA Vacutainers, gently inverted, and then mixed. The samples were centrifuged at 3,000 rpm (1,500 g) for 10 minutes at 4°C. The plasma matrix was collected into cryovials and frozen at −80°C until analysis. Copanlisib (and M1 metabolite) and niraparib plasma concentrations were quantified using validated tandem LC/MS-MS assays at a commercial analytic laboratory (NorthEast BioLab). The limit of quantitation was 0.5 ng/mL for copanlisib (and the M1 metabolite) and 3.74 ng/mL for niraparib. PK parameters for each analyte were determined by noncompartmental analysis methods using Phoenix WinNonlin 8.4 software (Certara USA Inc.).

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: Thirty patients were treated between May 2019 and March 2023. Table 1 displays patient demographics. Fifteen patients had endometrial cancer, and 15 patients had ovarian cancer. For patients with endometrial cancer, 7 (47%) had endometrioid histology, 4 (27%) had serous histology, and 4 (27%) had mixed histology. For patients with ovarian cancer, 14 (93%) had high-grade serous histology, whereas 1 patient had mixed epithelioid and clear-cell pathology. Only six patients (20%) had known germline (n = 4) or somatic (n = 2) BRCA mutations: four patients with ovarian cancer and two patients with endometrial cancer. Two patients with ovarian cancer were HRD without a germline BRCA mutation. Seven patients (23%) had somatic PTEN mutations, and six patients (20%) had somatic PIK3CA mutations. The overall representativeness of the trial is reported in Supplementary Table S3.

sec.title: RP2D determination
sec.p: Twenty-eight patients were evaluable for DLTs. Seventeen patients were enrolled in the dose escalation phase. Three patients were included in the DL1 cohort. In the first three patients, a DLT of grade 3 neutropenia occurred, and three additional patients were added to the DL1 cohort. An additional DLT of grade 3 hypertension was observed, and the cohort was expanded to nine patients in total, with no further DLTs occurring. Therefore, two out of nine patients experienced a DLT, and escalation proceeded to DL2 with a cohort of three patients. Two patients at DL2 experienced DLTs, both with grade 3 rash and grade 3 liver enzyme elevation. Therefore, de-escalation occurred to DL1A. Two of the two patients at DL1A experienced DLTs: one had a grade 3 rash and the other had an inability to take 75% of the planned dose due to grade 2 diarrhea. This level was deemed too toxic for further exploration. De-escalation to DL1 with three additional patients resulted in two DLTs: grade 3 mucositis and grade 3 rash. In total, 12 patients were enrolled in DL1, with three experiencing DLTs, which was deemed the putative RP2D.

An expansion cohort of 11 patients (seven with ovarian cancer and four with endometrial cancer) was enrolled to further evaluate tolerability. Three patients were treated at DL1 with one DLT, so an additional three patients were added to the cohort, two of whom experienced DLTs. De-escalation to DL−1) occurred, and three patients received this dose, one of whom experienced a DLT. Three additional patients were planned at DL−1, but after two patients were enrolled, another DLT occurred; the decision was made to stop enrollment in this study due to toxicity. Table 2 summarizes the DLTs that occurred at each DL.

sec.title: Adverse events
sec.p: AEs occurring in ≥20% of patients are summarized in Table 3. The most common DLT was a grade 3 maculopapular rash, which occurred in seven patients. Three patients were managed in the outpatient setting with a combination of oral methylprednisolone, oral doxycycline, topical triamcinolone cream, and/or topical clindamycin. One patient was diagnosed with drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) requiring hospitalization, and three other patients were hospitalized as well. These patients required treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone and topical steroids followed by a home prednisone taper. Given this significant AE/DLT, premedication was prescribed to the last four patients enrolled in the trial. Intravenous dexamethasone and intravenous diphenhydramine were given 30 minutes prior to copanlisib infusions. In addition, if a rash developed in the outpatient setting, it was treated urgently with a short course of oral steroids and/or topical steroids. Despite these interventions, two more patients experienced a DLT of rash, one of whom required hospitalization.

caption.p: AEs occurring in more than 20% of patients on trial.

sec.p: One patient died during the study after hospitalization for suspected bacterial versus marantic endocarditis and new pulmonary emboli. Following discharge, she experienced a middle cerebral artery stroke and ultimately died from disease progression and respiratory failure. This was deemed to be unrelated to the clinical trial. Another patient withdrew consent to pursue hospice.

sec.title: Response assessment and follow-up
sec.p: Twenty-four patients were evaluable for response. Six patients were excluded from response assessment due to early discontinuation because of AEs or DLTs (n = 3), patient withdrawal from the study (n = 2), and progression prior to receipt of two cycles (n = 1).

Of the 24 patients with response data, the ORR was 12.5% (95% CI, 2.7%–32.4%). Three patients had a best overall response of confirmed partial response: 2 out of 11 (18.2%) patients had endometrial cancer, and 1 out of 13 (7.7%) patients had ovarian cancer. However, one of these patients developed DRESS and discontinued the clinical trial after completing two cycles. Six additional patients had SD after four cycles. CBR was 37.5% (95% CI, 18.8%–59.4%). CBR in the endometrial cohort was 36.4% (95% CI, 10.9%–69.2%), and in the ovarian cohort, it was 38.5% (95% CI, 13.9%–68.4%). The median DOR for patients with clinical benefit was 7.4 months (IQR, 5.5–10.3; 95% CI, 4.6–10 months). See Fig. 2 for the response and response duration of each individual patient. Of the six patients with a BRCA mutation, one patient had clinical benefit, but the trial medications were discontinued due to grade 3 hypertension and rash.

sec.title: Translational studies
sec.p: WES downstream analysis was limited by sample size and is shown in Supplementary Fig. S1. Tumor samples from eight patients were analyzed by RPPA at baseline and after 28 days of therapy. Although there were 11 patients in the expansion cohort, three cases did not have matched on-treatment frozen tissue and were therefore excluded from RPPA analysis to ensure comparison only between paired pre- and on-treatment samples. We first examined changes in PI3K pathway signaling proteins in all tumors before and during treatment (Fig. 3A). We constructed a PI3K pathway activation score by averaging the expression levels of eleven proteins involved in PI3K activation and downstream signaling. For the group with SD (n = 3), PI3K scoring was relatively low even in two patient tumors that had known mutations in PI3K (either PIK3CA or PIK3C2B) prior to treatment (Fig. 3A) compared with tumors without PI3K mutations. In the PD group (n = 5), PI3K scoring was high in 3 out of 5 patient tumors despite only one of the three PI3K-high tumors harboring a PI3K mutation. Upon treatment, two out of 3 patient tumors with high PI3K scores in the PD group showed a decrease in their PI3K score. On the other hand, we observed increased PI3K scoring in PI3K score–low tumors in both the SD and PD groups, indicating the complexity of responses to multidrug treatment in patient tumors and possibly the inability to achieve a therapeutic dose secondary to toxicity.

caption.p: A, RPPA analysis of PI3K signaling in patient samples. The heatmap represents the protein expression related to PI3K signaling in patients with SD vs. PD in the pre- and on-treatment samples. A mutation indicates a tumor with mutations in PIK3CA or PIK3C2B. B, Identification of candidate therapy response predictors using RPPA. The heatmap shows proteins with significant differences in expression between SD and PD groups prior to starting treatment. A Student t test was used to identify significant differences between the groups (P < 0.05). Substrates of Akt are highlighted in red. PR, partial response.

sec.p: We next performed an unsupervised RPPA analysis to identify potential biomarkers predictive of response. As shown in Fig. 2B, 19 proteins were found to have a significant difference (P < 0.05) between the stable and PD groups, with four proteins being higher in the SD group and 15 in the PD group. In the PD group, many of the candidate biomarkers in the proteins with a significant difference in expression were substrates of Akt, a critical player in the PI3K pathway. These include phosphorylated forms of the ACLY, CREB, YAP, HSP27, and p27KIP1/CDKN1B proteins (Fig. 3B). Upon treatment, the expression patterns of these candidate biomarkers were largely altered (Supplementary Fig. S2).

The presence of multiple AKT substrates within differentially expressed proteins between SD and PD samples prompted us to perform a systematic study on potential pathway changes between the two sample groups. To this end, we compiled 29 pathways presented in the RPPA platform (see “Patients and Methods”) and conducted a GSEA pathway analysis (Fig. 4). The results confirmed that AKT substrates are significantly enriched in the PD group. Additionally, although not statistically significant, a trend toward enrichment of Ser/Thr kinases and MTOR signaling components was observed. Notably, the PI3K–AKT–MTOR signaling pathway did not show differential activation between the SD and PD groups, which is consistent with the PI3K score mutation status results. GSEA also suggested a potential higher activity within the hypoxia and focal adhesion pathways in the SD group (statistically insignificant).

caption.p: RPPA pathway analysis on pretreated SD and PD samples. A, GSEA pathway analysis on 29 pathway alterations between SD and PD samples. B, GSEA enrichment plots on the top five changed pathways between SD and PD samples, as well as the PI3K–AKT–MTOR signaling pathway. NES, normalized enrichment score.

sec.title: PK
sec.p: The PK parameters for copanlisib and niraparib were evaluated on day 15 of cycle 1 using samples collected up to 24 hours after the start of administration from 16 patients who received the study medications at three different DLs, as summarized in Table 4. Of note, among the six patients in the copanlisib 45 mg and niraparib 100 mg DL, the dose of niraparib was reduced from 200 to 100 mg before day 15 of cycle 1 in three patients. Thus, their blood collection and subsequent PK analysis were completed while receiving the lowered DL. Due to limited sampling up to 24 hours, the calculated PK parameters and evaluable data for both copanlisib and niraparib were limited within this constraint.

sec.p: The mean observed maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) for copanlisib after a 1-hour intravenous infusion was 402, 447, and 436 ng/mL for DLs 1, −1, and 1A, respectively. The calculated half-life and exposure (AUC0–24) over the 24-hour period for copanlisib were 21.7, 15.4, and 10.2 hours and 1,531; 1,813; and 1,404 ng/mL × hours, respectively. The mean normalized AUC0–24 [(ng × hours/mL)/kg] to body weight was consistent among the three DLs: 22.85, 21.7, and 23.76, respectively. The mean observed Cmax for niraparib after oral administration of niraparib capsules was 642, 332, and 328 for DLs 1, −1, and 1A, respectively. The half-life and AUCinf were 31.2, 51 hours, and 26,542, 18,683 ng/mL × hours for DLs 1 and −1, respectively.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study evaluated the combination of copanlisib (pan-class I PI3K inhibitor) and niraparib (PARP-1 and PARP-2 inhibitor) in patients with recurrent endometrial or ovarian cancer. The rationale for this study stemmed from preclinical models demonstrating synergistic effects between these two drugs (44, 45). The overall ORR was 12.5%, and the CBR was 34.8%, with a median DOR of 7.4 months. However, treatment success was limited by dermatologic toxicity. Prior studies of monotherapy niraparib report a CBR of 20% in endometrial cancer (26) and an ORR of 21% in BRCA-mutant or HRD ovarian cancers as maintenance therapy (17).

Combinations of PARPis and PI3K pathway inhibitors have been studied previously. A phase I trial in recurrent breast and ovarian cancer combined the oral pan-PI3K inhibitor buparlisib with olaparib (54). Toxicities related to the PI3K inhibitor prevented significant dose escalation, and no additional benefit was noted from the addition of buparlisib to outcomes from prior studies of PARPi alone. Another phase I trial looked at this combination in both recurrent ovarian and breast cancer populations using an alpha-specific PI3K inhibitor, alpelisib, and olaparib (55). This trial reported significant improvements in tolerance to this combination, but response rates were comparable with those of PARPi monotherapy in patients with platinum-resistant, BRCA wild-type epithelial ovarian cancers. The possible improvement in tolerance of PI3K inhibitors could be related to alpha-specific inhibition rather than pan-inhibition, as in this trial.

Translational analyses, though limited by sample size, yielded several insights. RPPA data showed that PI3K scores decreased in some tumors with initially high pretreatment signaling—consistent with effective copanlisib target inhibition—yet these changes did not correlate with clinical response. Our best candidate response predictors from the RPPA were ARID1A and p27KIP1. High ARID1A protein expression was uniformly observed in patients with PD, whereas those with SD exhibited minimal ARID1A expression. This inverse relationship aligns with prior research, which shows that loss of ARID1A sensitizes tumor cells to PARP inhibition, suggesting that tumors retaining high ARID1A expression may be less responsive to this combination (56, 57). A downstream substrate of AKT, p27, also had elevated expression in all patients with PD. Although we could not directly adjust for tumor purity, systematic differences in tumor content are unlikely to fully explain these findings. Interestingly, prior research has correlated low levels of p27 expression with poor survival outcomes in ovarian and other cancers (58, 59). In total, five Akt-related substrates, including p27, were significantly elevated in the PD group, supporting the hypothesis that Akt pathway activation, rather than PI3K status, predicts poor response. Although this study does not formally distinguish between predictive and prognostic biomarkers, taken together, our results suggest that a combination of Akt substrates may serve as a promising biomarker for copanlisib, as well as for other, more tolerable PI3K inhibitors in combination with PARPi therapy. These findings underscore the importance of Akt status rather than PI3K status in predicting patient response in this combination.

The collection of blood samples for PK assessment of copanlisib and niraparib in our clinical study was limited to 24 hours after the start of administration of both agents on day 15 of cycle 1. As reported in a prior single-agent study, the circulating half-life of copanlisib was 38.2 hours, which is much longer than in our cohorts. With limited sampling up to 24 hours, the calculated half-life ranged from 10 to 21 hours (60). From this, we can infer that our data describe copanlisib up to the initial (alpha) elimination phase for most patients who have yet to reach the terminal (beta) elimination phase; thus, estimation of the terminal clearance rate was not possible. The PK analysis of niraparib was more constrained, not only due to limited blood sampling but also due to the added effects of oral administration and absorption. PK analysis was successful in only 8 out of 16 available patient datasets, with 7 in the DL1 cohort. The normalized-dose AUC0–inf of niraparib for DL1 was elevated compared with a single agent of niraparib in two separate reports (61, 62). Thus, the combination of niraparib and copanlisib resulted in a 1.89-fold increase in niraparib exposure compared with the AUCs of niraparib as a single agent.

Often, when evaluating potential drug–drug interactions, most of the focus is on the cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoenzyme, as these isoenzymes account for the metabolism of approximately 90% of all medications. As niraparib undergoes hydrolysis of its amide moiety via hepatic carboxylesterases (hCE), this metabolic pathway is often underappreciated as a potential route for drug–drug interactions (34). Some common prescription medications that also undergo this same hydrolysis metabolism via hCE include angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, antihyperlipidemic agents, antivirals, immunosuppressants, antispasmodics, centrally acting agents (central nervous system), anticoagulants, and anticancer agents (63). In our PK patient population, a review of their concomitant medications revealed multiple therapeutic agents that share the same hCE metabolism pathway as niraparib, in addition to CYP3A4 inhibition by copanlisib, which may be responsible for an increase in the AUC for both agents, particularly with niraparib (Supplementary Table S4). In addition to many medications that share the CYP3A4 metabolic pathway, simvastatin and atorvastatin were two lipid-lowering agents taken by some of our patients, which may contribute to the partial inhibition of niraparib metabolism. Thus, in general, it would be highly prudent to fully evaluate all concomitant medications that our patients may be taking, not only by CYP450 pathways but also by other lesser-known pathways, such as hCEs.

In summary, the combination of copanlisib and niraparib had comparable response rates with PARPi monotherapy but was associated with significant dermatologic toxicity, precluding advancement to a planned phase II study. Future research should consider validating biomarkers in larger cohorts for PI3K/AKT-targeting agents in combination with PARPis and focus on developing more tolerable regimens.
